processing: Green tea: shoots are spread to wither, fired to stop the enzymes, rolled lightly, fired again in a pan, straightened into strands and dried until firm, keeping the down and a fresh character.
harvest_season: Spring, from early April into May; the mountain gardens are high and cool so the main picking is around Grain Rain, with a smaller pre-Qingming crop from lower slopes.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly flattened strands in a glossy green with silvery buds partly showing.
appearance_wet: Even bud-and-leaf sets, tender and bright.
taste_profile: Crisp and sweet with fresh chestnut, a hint of orchid and a cool, mineral finish; lighter than Longjing but with a longer aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 80–85 °C. Mountain leaf: it stands a fourth steep where lowland bud teas fade.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, mostly from around Grain Rain for the high gardens; pre-Qingming lots exist from lower slopes and cost more. Production is small and mostly sold within Zhejiang. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Tianmu Qing Ding is the green tea of Tianmu Mountain in Lin'an, west of Hangzhou, a high, forested range with old temples and ancient trees and a cooler, later spring than the West Lake hills an hour away. The name means 'green peak'. It is an old tea district by local account, and today it is a small-production mountain green that locals prize and few outsiders have tasted.

It is made from the local seed-grown bushes: fired, lightly rolled, fired again, straightened into slightly flat strands and dried gently, so it sits between the flat Longjing style and the curled styles in look, and keeps a fresh rather than toasty character.

The cup is crisp and sweet, chestnut and a little orchid, with a cool, almost mineral finish that lasts longer than its light body suggests, the signature of high, cool gardens. It takes 80–85 °C in a gaiwan and gives four steeps, with the second the best. People who find Longjing too toasty and Mao Feng too soft tend to land here happily.

Because the mountain is high, the main harvest comes around Grain Rain in late April, and most of it is sold within Zhejiang as the current spring's tea. If you see 'Tianmu' tea in early March, it is from lower slopes or from somewhere else entirely. Ask for elevation and picking date, and expect the price to sit below Xihu Longjing and above everyday Zhejiang greens.

Lin'an is also known for its hickory nuts, and a dish of them roasted goes well with this tea, as any toasted nut does.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. Revival 'from the 1980s' follows the usual Chinese account; exact dates vary by source.
history:
Tianmu Qing Ding, also called Tianmu Yunwu, comes from the Tianmu range in Lin'an, northwest of Hangzhou. Local accounts say Tianmu tea was already known in the Tang, more than 1,200 years ago, and went as tribute in the Ming, though these claims rest on later retellings.

The recent record is plainer. From the mid-1990s some of the gardens went into organic production for export, including to Europe, and the name was registered as a national geographical indication in 2012, held by the Lin'an tea association. Little else about its modern development is documented in detail.
